description: At 11:30 a.m. on February 1, 2019, an employee was working for a firm that made custom signs, such as menu boards, real estate signs, fascia, and lighting accent bands. The worksite was a one-story freestanding industrial warehouse in a light industrial zone. The building comprised administrative offices and a warehouse with a large fenced yard. The worksite had one employer. All workers were employees of the company. At the time of inspection, the company was in the process of closing the business due to a downturn in the economy. There were no employees at the worksite at the time of inspection. The last day employees worked per the employer was February 15, 2019. The manufacturing involved the use of metalworking machinery and woodworking machinery. This included but not limited to punch presses, press brakes, table saws, and chop saws. The injured worker had worked for the company for nearly ten years as a shop laborer. He had been hired in 2008. The worker had regularly operated the machinery to fabricate signs and parts. On the day of the incident, the worker was operating a 90-kilonewton (10-ton) Rousselle punch press to make holes in a bracket. The bracket was made of steel and approximately 3.175 millimeters (0.125 inches) thick. The holes were approximately 9.525 millimeters (0.375 inches) in diameter. The design called for one hole on each side of the L-bracket. The punch die was a single operation C-frame die, which was secured to the bolster plate on the bed of the punch press. The die had feed clearance for the 3.175-millimeter (0.125-inch) thick bracket. The punch tip was in an enclosed throat. In practice, the employee would place the bracket into the feed slot in the die and engage the foot pedal to operate the press. The employee would then manually turn the bracket 45 degrees, and the second side would be punched. On the day of the incident, the employee had not completed setting up of the press opening or cycle setting before he engaged the foot pedal as he adjusted the placement of the bracket in the die. The press cycled and caught the middle and first fingers on the employee's left hand under the metal bracket. Those two fingers were crushed. The incident occurred at 11:30 a.m. on February 1, 2019. The employer reported the incident to the Division at approximately 12:17 p.m. At that time, the employer was uncertain if the employee had suffered an amputation. The Huntington Beach pinch point Department reported the accident to the Division at approximately 12:28 p.m. on the same day, also uncertain if the employee had suffered an amputation or not. The employee was transported to UCI medical center for treatment. He was not hospitalized. Following a later request by the Division, the hospital did not find any mediical records for the employee. The injured worker was supervised by the owner, but the owner did not witness the incident. The inspection found that the punch press did not have required guarding at the point of operation. This was cited accordingly. The violation was cited as accident related. This was cited accordingly. The violation was cited as accident related, the guard was reinstalled.

description: October 2, 2021: during a line ride, an oil sheen was detected off the coastline and reported to the platform personnel at approximately 8:00 am PT. Upon notification of the oil sheen, platform personnel initiated the Oil Spill Response Plan and notified regulatory agencies. On October 3, it was announced that a Unified Command was established to respond to the oil spill. The cause, timing, and details regarding the spill are currently being investigated and this information is preliminary. Cause Update, 3-17-22: During a large winter storm on January 25, 2021, the two supertankers were driven by winds and waves and drug their anchors across the seafloor and into areas where federal law prohibits anchoring. As the two supertankers dragged their anchors, both anchors hooked onto the concrete-encased pipeline and dragged a 4,000-foot section of the pipeline across the seafloor. The anchor-dragging bent and bowed the pipeline, displacing some parts of the pipeline by more than 100 feet and breaking off the concrete casing around the pipeline. Neither vessel nor the Marine Exchange of Southern California, responsible for managing ship positions in the harbor, informed anyone at Beta or Amplify that there was an anchor dragging incident across the exclusion zone. Timing Update 3-17-22: Over the course of the later afternoon and evening of October 1, the offshore platform and onshore pipeline personnel worked together to troubleshoot and rectify what were believed to be false leak detection system alarms. Following each alarm, the crews investigated various components of the platform and the pipeline's instrumentalities to determine what could be contributing to what were thought to be false alarms. Unbeknownst to the crew during this period, and further complicating their efforts, however, was the fact that the pipeline's leak detection system was not functioning as designed, but was repeatedly and wrongly signaling a potential leak at the platform where no leak could be detected by the platform personnel and where no leak was occurring. Instead, as the factual record shows today, the leak occurred over four miles away, where the pipeline had been displaced more than 100 feet by a ship's anchor - a fact not shared with knowledge of that anchor -dragging incident. Had the crew known there was an actual oil spill in the water, they would have shut down the pipeline immediately. When a line ride the morning of October 2 identified a sheen in the water, the Company immediately began to execute its federally-approved oil spill response plan. description: Renaissance Offshore, LLC production complex experienced a small gas leak that required manual shut down of components Compressors Recip. and Turbine Compressor. On April 1, 2031 at approximately 16:35 hours, a small gas leak was discovered proactively while personnel were making rounds. A crew member discovered a small gas leak on the CAE-2601 (C-159) centrifugal turbine's center housing between the housing and discharge capsule assembly. The small gas leak was not detected by the Turbine Compressor Building's Enclosure sensing devices lower or upper limits (Gas Detectors). The small leak was contained within a Class I div. 0 area, and due to its size, being proactively identified by crew member no further escalation took place. When the small leak was discovered, a calibrated portable gas detector was used to verify gas concentration lower and upper ranges in relation to Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) concentrations. At ~12" away from the leak point, the lower ALM range registered and as sensor was moved closer to the actual location, the upper ALM range was denoted. The leak was approximately ~ 3.4' from an insulated exhaust system with ~ 1151 degrees protected. UWA was contacted, and a manual shut down response was conducted, the concern was the proximity to a nearby hot surfaces or if the leak progressed. The unit was successfully repaired, seals replaced, re-torqued, and placed back-in-service. No injuries, pollution, or damages occurred as the result of the small gas leak; no need for emergency musters, with the harness properly secured.

description: On a Rig facility within the Ewing Bank Area, a floorhand traversed over the top of hand rail on charging excavator deck, in an attempt to access elevatoring work platform approximately 6 foot below. A ladder was not able to be installed to access the scaffolding work platform in this location. IP utilized the outside of the handrail to climb down to scaffold platform below. During the descent to the platform , IP's foot slipped causing a fall. Harness and lanyard stopped the fall after approximately 6 foot. IP was able to self-rescue by standing up on scaffolding platform below. Reported to medic on board with unspecified back pain. No other cuts/abrasions/bruising from fall. IP was flown by regular helicopter and being brought to Dr for further evaluation by his company HSE representative. Medical evaluation by an occupational medicine clinic found no internal injury. However, MRI confirmed that IP has pre-existing multiple-level degenerative disc disease. Further investigation into the incident have reclassified the incident as "Alleged Fall From Heights - First Aid". Noteworthy findings as follows: - No personnel witnessed the alleged event. Co-worker for task was on the lower processing deck with his back to the IP during the alleged event timeframe. - IP's weight and distance of claimed fall would be very likely to result in superficial/topical injuries at the contact points of the harness (i.e. inner thighs). No injuries/indications found. - The harness was evaluated for signs of involvement in a fall. The lanyards showed no indications of fall arrest (energy absorber deployment), nor were there any other indications of involvement of the harness in a fall arrest event. - All medical evaluations resulted in no identification of injury associated with a fall arrest event. IP was determined to suffer from chronic condition (degenerative disc disease), for which he will seek continued care from his personal physician. - The culmination of all diagnostic/evaluative processes and procedures was a full duty release with no restrictions.
